stories.title: 70,000 left EDs before full treatment in seven months
stories.summary: More than 70,100 people did not wait, or left before completing their treatment, in emergency departments during the first seven months of this year, new figures show. The issue was most prominent at the Mater and St James's hospitals in Dublin. There were also 31,821 patients who waited longer than 24 hours to be admitted, or discharged, in emergency departments. The data was obtained from the HSE under a parliamentary question, submitted by chairperson of the Oireachtas Committee on Health, Social Democrats TD Pádraig Rice. It showed that the average waiting time in emergency departments for patients between January and July was 9.3 hours. The Dublin South East Region performed best, with over 67% of patients admitted or discharged in six hours.

stories.title: Orange warnings as Storm Austen to bring 'intense rain'
stories.summary: Two Status Orange rain warnings have been issued for six counties as Storm Austen is set to hit Ireland this evening. Met Éireann said there could be disruption and delays to public transport, flooding and very difficult travelling conditions as intense rain is forecast. A Status Orange rain warning will be in effect for Cork, Kerry and Waterford from 10pm until 5am tomorrow. A separate Status Orange rain warning has been issued for Dublin, Wexford and Wicklow. This warning will be in operation from 2am to 8am tomorrow. A Status Yellow warning for wind and rain will also be in effect for all counties from 7pm until 10am tomorrow. Met Éireann meteorologist Mark Bowe said Storm Austen is heading towards the southern part of the UK, bringing strong winds along with very heavy rain, which will then sweep across the southern part of Ireland.

stories.title: UK government approves drilling in Jackdaw gas field
stories.summary: The UK government has approved plans to begin drilling in the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. The decision by the North Sea Transition Authority ends months of speculation about the future of the project, which owner Adura said could deliver around 6% of UK North Sea gas production. Britain's Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, who gave approval for the NSTA to grant consent for drilling, said the move will "support the country's energy security with homegrown gas this winter". Prime Minister Andy Burnham added the decision will "protect hundreds of jobs and help keep millions of homes warm", but stressed it would not hinder the government’s targets on renewable energy. The drilling project is one of two - alongside the Rosebank oil field off Shetland - which were approved by the previous Conservative government. Both were approved for drilling licences in June 2022, but this was overturned by the Scottish courts after a challenge from environmental campaigners.

stories.title: Europe car sales rise 10% in September amid EV surge
stories.summary: Strong demand for electrified cars helped Europe's new-car market grow in September, offsetting another sharp decline in petrol and diesel vehicle sales, data from the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association showed today. New-car registrations, a proxy for sales, rose 10.2% year-on-year to 1.36 million vehicles across the European Union, Britain and the European Free Trade Association, ACEA said. Demand for electrified vehicles remained strong across major European markets, supported by purchase incentives and a broader model lineup. Battery-electric, plug-in hybrid and hybrid car registrations jumped 59.9%, 24% and 5.3%, respectively, and together accounted for 76.2% of all new vehicles. But petrol and diesel registrations fell 20.6% and 28.2%, today's figures show. Chinese automakers continued to gain ground, with Chery and BYD nearly tripling and doubling sales, respectively, while Geely and SAIC reported increases of more than 33% and 23%.

stories.title: Australian MP loses both legs after car attack
stories.summary: Australian MP Helen Haines, who was deliberately hit by a car on Monday, has had both her legs amputated following the attack, her husband said. Phil Haines said his wife had her left leg amputated on Monday and while there had been hope that her other leg could be saved, a second amputation was carried out today. "But the good news in all this is Helen is alive and she's stable. That is the most important thing for our family. "The two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind. Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person." Mr Haines added that he was "overwhelmed" by the support the family had received since the alleged attack. Ms Haines, an independent politician who has championed causes including climate change and regional housing, was hit by the car outside ⁠her electoral office in Wangaratta, northeast of Melbourne.

stories.title: Carrick: 'I've not given my position any thought'
stories.summary: Under-pressure Michael Carrick claims not to have given his position any thought after a humiliating Champions League loss at Como that saw him apologise to Manchester United fans and question his players. An awful start to the season reached a nadir on Wednesday evening in Italy, where the Red Devils' winless run stretched to a seventh successive match in all competitions for the first time since 2015. Cesc Fabregas’ Como outplayed United from the outset, with burgeoning star Nico Paz’s brace complemented by Tasos Douvikas and Jacobo Ramon goals before substitute Joshua Zirkzee scored a stoppage-time consolation. Under-fire boss Carrick held his hands up apologetically to the largely empty away end at the Stadio Giuseppe Sinigaglia after a damaging 4-1 loss that puts his position in jeopardy. "First of all, I have to apologise to the supporters," the United boss said. "I went over to the (away) end, and I care about this football club as much as anyone, if not more with the position that I’m in and what I value this football club.

stories.title: Arteta admits final defeat is still driving him
stories.summary: Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta admits the lingering pain of last season's Champions League final defeat is fuelling his desire for European glory and rejected suggestions his team are "boring". The Premier League champions face Bayern Munich at the Allianz Arena this evening in their biggest test since losing to Paris St Germain on penalties in May. Asked if he had moved on from the agonising shootout loss to PSG, Arteta said: "I tried, but I haven’t managed to. "I tried for many weeks during the summer, but when I see the ball, the scenes, I hear the music, I want it so badly. "We know that we have to go step by step, but I think that fire is within the team and all of us individually. "We know what we had to go through – not being champions of Europe by a penalty. So, let’s try again."

stories.title: Nankivell's new Munster deal paves way for Ireland career
stories.summary: Centre Alex Nankivell has signed a two-year contract extension with Munster that will tie him to the province until 2029. The 29-year-old joined from the Chiefs in the summer of 2023 and has spoken publicly of the possibility of representing Ireland at international level. Nankivell will be 32 when he completes World Rugby's residency rules in 2028. He played five games for the Maoris and four for All Blacks XV and said recently that playing international rugby again is the "dream". Nankivell has made 58 appearances for the province since joining three years ago, immediately established himself as a key member of the squad, scoring three tries in 19 appearances in his first campaign in red. His all-action displays saw the New Zealander quickly establish himself as a fans’ favourite, though a hamstring injury saw his second season restricted to 15 starts for the province.

stories.title: Fearless! On Vincent Browne's Magill and Ireland in the 1980s
stories.summary: We present an extract from Fearless! Vincent Browne's Magill and Ireland in the 1980s, the new book by Kevin Rafter. This book is not just the story of a magazine. It's the history of a crucial and contentious decade in Irish life. The 1980s were years of political turbulence, economic decline and bitter referendums on abortion and divorce. Magill and its founding editor, Vincent Browne, was at the heart of all these stories. Kevin Rafter uncovers the drama behind Magill, from its launch in 1977 to becoming a publication that the Sunday Times said dragged Irish journalism out of its 'comfortable, questioning dullness'. With Colm Tóibín’s resignation at the start of 1985, Vincent Browne had planned to quickly recruit a new editor. The initial plan was dashed when several journalists, including Damien Kiberd, then at the Irish Press, turned him down. His difficult reputation put off several potential candidates. The position was advertised in March 1985. The successful applicant was required to be ‘a journalist of outstanding calibre and drive’ and someone who would ‘consolidate the success that has been achieved by the outgoing editor and give a new impetus to the magazine’. The role came with a ‘highly attractive salary’ and the possibility of share options. Interested applicants were asked to apply in confidence. After confirming his exit, Tóibín called Mark Brennock, who was working at Magill. Tóibín predicted that Browne would have work for the young journalist, especially as the magazine would shortly start publishing every two weeks. ‘He [Browne] will need somebody to get the magazine out,’ Tóibín said. In this period of editorial change, Browne was listed as ‘managing editor’ but the real work in getting the magazine through the production cycle was undertaken by Brennock, who stepped in as ‘production editor’. Gene Kerrigan and Olivia O’Leary were listed as ‘assistant editors’ (O’Leary departed in May 1985). Ahead of meetings with Browne to discuss Magill, Brennock and Kerrigan would talk through their editorial plans. Browne was pleased to hear that the source of Charlie Haughey’s money was on the list. During these months, Browne and Derek Dunne wrote a cover story on the IRA’s finances (21 March 1985), while Browne also penned a lengthy analysis of the INLA (August 1985).The first of Gene Kerrigan’s seminal works on the Kerry Babies scandal was the main cover lead in the 30 May 1985 issue. It was also a year of significant sporting achievements for Irish athletics. The public’s interest in these successes saw several sporting front-cover stories, including Ireland’s Triple Crown-winning rugby team (4 April 1985), world champion boxer Barry McGuigan (13 June 1985) and cyclist Seán Kelly, who had attained the rank of world number one in his sport (August 1985). The new fortnightly schedule promised more coverage of stories ‘which tended to get squeezed out for space reasons in the monthly format’ and a new review section giving greater attention to arts and entertainment. The move coincided with the launch of a new weekly magazine, the Magill TV Guide. Like the motivation behind Status some years previously, the new weekly title was to share overheads with the now fortnightly Magill. Both magazines operated out of the Merrion Row offices. For different reasons, however, neither initiative was successful. In the case of Magill the editorial budget was not available to support a fortnightly publication cycle. Having been introduced in March 1985, the twice-monthly project lasted only until the end of June 1985 (across nine issues) before being abandoned. The magazine returned to being a monthly publication from August 1985.

With Colm Tóibín’s [[éirí as|resignation]] at the start of 1985, Vincent Browne had planned to quickly [[earcach|recruit]] a new [[atheagraí|editor]]. The initial [[plean|plan]] was dashed when several [[iriseoirí|journalists]], including Damien Kiberd, then at the Irish Press, turned him down. His [[doiciúil|difficult]] reputation put off several potential [[iarrthóirí|candidates]]. The position was [[fógartha|advertised]] in March 1985. The [[rathúil|successful]] applicant was required to be ‘a [[iriseoir|journalist]] of outstanding [[calabra|calibre]] and drive’ and [[duine|someone]] who would ‘consolidate the [[rath|success]] that has been achieved by the outgoing [[atheagraí|editor]] and give a [[nua|new]] impetus to the magazine’. The [[ról|role]] came with a ‘highly attractive [[tuarastal|salary]]’ and the [[féidearthacht|possibility]] of share [[roghanna|options]]. Interested applicants were [[iarrtha|asked]] to apply in [[muinín|confidence]]. After confirming his [[amach|exit]], Tóibín called Mark Brennock, who was working at Magill. Tóibín predicted that Browne would have work for the young [[iriseoir|journalist]], especially as the magazine would [[go gairid|shortly]] start publishing every two [[seachtainí|weeks]]. ‘He [Browne] will need [[duine éigin|somebody]] to get the [[armlann|magazine]] out,’ Tóibín said. In this [[tréimhse|period]] of editorial [[athrú|change]], Browne was [[liostaithe|listed]] as ‘managing editor’ but the real [[obair|work]] in getting the [[armlann|magazine]] through the production [[ciogal|cycle]] was undertaken by Brennock, who stepped in as ‘production [[atheagraí|editor]]’. Gene Kerrigan and Olivia O’Leary were [[liostaithe|listed]] as ‘assistant [[eagarthóirí|editors]]’ (O’Leary departed in May 1985). Ahead of [[comhordúcháin|meetings]] with Browne to discuss Magill, Brennock and Kerrigan would talk [[trí|through]] their editorial [[pleananna|plans]]. Browne was pleased to [[clois|hear]] that the [[foinse|source]] of Charlie Haughey’s [[airgead|money]] was on the [[liosta|list]]. During these months, Browne and Derek Dunne wrote a cover [[scéal|story]] on the IRA’s [[airgead|finances]] (21 March 1985), while Browne also penned a lengthy [[anailís|analysis]] of the INLA (August 1985).The first of Gene Kerrigan’s seminal [[monarcha|works]] on the Kerry Babies [[scannal|scandal]] was the main [[brat|cover]] lead in the 30 May 1985 [[atheagrú|issue]]. It was also a [[bliain|year]] of significant sporting [[éachtaí|achievements]] for Irish athletics. The public’s [[leas|interest]] in these [[rath|successes]] saw several sporting front-cover [[scéalta|stories]], including Ireland’s Triple Crown-winning rugby [[foireann|team]] (4 April 1985), world [[curadh|champion]] boxer Barry McGuigan (13 June 1985) and [[rothaí|cyclist]] Seán Kelly, who had attained the [[borb|rank]] of world [[líon|number]] one in his [[spórt|sport]] (August 1985). The new [[coicíseán|fortnightly]] schedule promised more coverage of [[scéalta|stories]] ‘which tended to [[faigh|get]] squeezed out for [[spás|space]] reasons in the monthly [[formáid|format]]’ and a new review [[alt|section]] giving greater attention to [[ealaíona|arts]] and entertainment. The [[aistriú|move]] coincided with the [[lainse|launch]] of a [[nua|new]] weekly magazine, the Magill TV Guide. Like the [[inspreagadh|motivation]] behind Status some [[blianta|years]] previously, the new weekly [[teideal|title]] was to share [[forchostas|overheads]] with the now [[coicíseán|fortnightly]] Magill. Both magazines [[d'oibrigh|operated]] out of the Merrion Row offices. For different [[cúiseanna|reasons]], however, neither initiative was [[rathúil|successful]]. In the case of Magill the editorial [[buiséad|budget]] was not [[ar fáil|available]] to support a fortnightly [[foilsiú|publication]] cycle. Having been introduced in March 1985, the twice-monthly [[tionscadal|project]] lasted only until the end of June 1985 (across nine [[easláinte|issues]]) before being abandoned. The [[armlann|magazine]] returned to being a monthly [[foilsiú|publication]] from August 1985.

stories.title: Normal People stars back Sally Rooney in open letter
stories.summary: Normal People stars Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones have signed an open letter supporting Irish author Sally Rooney after her publisher stopped supplying her books in the UK. The actors, who played Connell and Marianne in the television adaptation of Rooney's bestselling novel, are joined by the show’s director Lenny Abrahamson and Conversations with Friends star Alison Oliver. The letter, published in the New Statesman on Wednesday, declares: "Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public." It criticises the UK legislation that has led to the decision to stop supplying Rooney’s books, describing it as an affront to freedom of expression. The signatories call on the UK government to amend the legislation, rejecting what they describe as "direct or indirect" censorship. Other Irish figures to sign the letter include Jessie Buckley and Sharon Horgan, CMAT, Kneecap and writers Marian Keyes, Colm Tóibín, Anne Enright, Colum McCann and Anna Burns.

stories.title: The bride wore black: Irish woman on her black-themed wedding
stories.summary: Crows, skulls, black roses and a double coffin... No, these aren't Halloween decorations but the dazzling decor at a recent wedding in Trim Castle, where the bride and entire wedding party wore black. Alternative weddings and especially wedding looks are trending across bridal sites lately, from wedding gowns in all shades of colours and unusual settings chosen over the traditional church. But as bride Keelin Ward puts it, it could never have been anything but this for her big day. "Because that's me and I was just being myself", she told Callan. "That’s what I love. What’s tradition anyway? I like to do things my own way." Ward joins a long list of brides who opted for something particularly eye-catching for her nuptials, such as Dita Von Teese, who married Marilyn Manson in a shimmering purple taffeta design by Vivienne Westwood for their wedding at Gottfried Helnwein's Castle in County Tipperary, or Gwen Stefani, who wore an ombre pink and white design by John Galliano to marry Gavin Rossdale. Ward's dress was designed and made by Niamh Lynch from Bespoke Bridal in Marley Park, she said. "I told her exactly what I wanted; I just wanted black lace. There was a built-in corset as well; I wanted a high neck on it, a very dramatic train on the back and long lace sleeves." Next, it was designing the space in Trim Castle, and Ward turned to Charlene Waldron at Elegant Events.

stories.title: Sentencing of man who punched Brendan Courtney adjourned
stories.summary: The sentence hearing of a man who punched broadcaster Brendan Courtney several times has been adjourned to allow his suitability for community service to be assessed. Ross Deegan, 22, of An Riasc, Finglas, Dublin 11 pleaded guilty to assaulting Mr Courtney causing harm on 27 February 2025, at Usher's Quay in Dublin city centre. Dublin Circuit Criminal Court previously heard that Mr Courtney was walking home along the quays around 9.30pm on 27 February 2025, when he was beckoned over to a car stopped at traffic lights. The court heard the front passenger appeared to roll down the window and call him over. Mr Courtney went over thinking he knew the occupants of the car and later described to gardaí that he believed they were ridiculing him. Deegan, who was a back seat passenger, left the vehicle, then assaulted Mr Courtney along with a co-accused, who is also before the courts. Mr Courtney went to hospital the following day after waking up in pain. He sustained a concussion and a fracture of his eye socket.

stories.title: Do you know your rights if your next flight is cancelled or delay
stories.summary: Analysis: Whether it's flying local or further afield, a cancelled flight usually sees people walking away from money they're legally owed A cancelled flight is stressful enough without wondering whether you're owed anything for it. According to the Irish Aviation Authority, almost half of Irish passengers don't actually know. A survey by Amárach Research for the IAA found just 53% were confident they knew their rights when a flight is delayed or cancelled, while 33% weren't sure and 14% had no idea at all. For a country where flying is how most of us get anywhere - whether that's a short domestic hop, a weekend in Europe or the long haul home from further afield - that's a lot of people who could be walking away from money they're legally owed. Because knowing your rights and getting what you're owed are two different things. In 2025, the IAA upheld 1,213 complaints against airlines, resulting in over €1.1 million paid out in refunds and compensation - money that went to passengers who knew to ask. The authority has now launched a "Know Your Rights" awareness campaign to close that gap before winter disruption arrives. Under EU Regulation 261/2004, the rules are more generous than most people assume. Clare Mulcahy, the IAA's head of consumer affairs, put it plainly: "if your flight is delayed you're entitled to meals, refreshments, hotel accommodation if necessary". If it's cancelled, "you have the choice of a refund or a re-route plus care and assistance while you're waiting." Compensation ranges from €250 to €600 depending on flight length and notice given. The same rules apply whether you're flying between Dublin and Donegal or going long-haul out of Dublin, Cork or Shannon, as long as the airline caused the disruption.

stories.summary: A US Democratic party congressional candidate has been detained in the occupied-West Bank by Israeli forces, along with dozens of activists who were picking olives alongside Palestinian farmers, rights groups said. Israeli organisation Rabbis for Human Rights said around 80 volunteers, including Brad Lander, were detained by Israeli military and police on village farmland near Bethlehem where for about two hours they had been accompanying the Palestinian farmers. Israeli forces informed the group they were in a closed military zone and detained them before taking them to a police station, Rabbis for Human Rights said in a statement. stories.title: Kilkenny's Joyce to depart Brisbane Lions
stories.summary: Kilkenny's Darragh Joyce's AFL future is up in the air as Premiership champions Brisbane Lions confirmed that they will not be offering him a new contract. The Rower–Inistioge hurler joined St Kilda as a category B international rookie and played 13 AFL games for the Saints over six years. Joyce then joined the Lions through the AFL pre-season supplemental selection period ahead of the 2023 season. The 29-year-old played five games in his first season and six the next as he became an important member of their defensive roster. Having failed to make an AFL appearance in 2025, Joyce featured three times in 2026 as the Lions completed a remarkable AFL Grand Final turnaround against Freemantle; Joyce failed to earn selection for that showpiece at the MCG. "Darragh's experience, resilience, and willingness to put the team first have been greatly appreciated," Lions general manager Danny Daly told the club website.

stories.title: Regulator would have 'power' to force City owner to sell
stories.summary: The Independent Football Regulator will have "absolute power" to force Manchester City's owners to sell if they are ultimately found to have run the club improperly, the watchdog's chair has said. City have been found guilty of circumventing Premier League rules by an independent commission, which found they set up "sham" commercial arrangements to inflate revenues or reduce costs by over £900m over a nine-season period. They were also found to have made "concerted efforts" to "stop and frustrate" the Premier League's investigation into those arrangements. David Kogan, the chair of the IFR, told 'The Rest Is Football' podcast it was premature to talk about any action his organisation might take, with City having lodged an appeal against the original commission's verdict. However, he confirmed the IFR had the power to force a sale by the club's owner Sheikh Mansour if that was felt to be appropriate. "We have the power to ask an owner to step away from a club if we believe that they run a club in a way that is neither fit, fair or done with propriety," Kogan said.

stories.title: Flannery named as Lions Women's head of operations
stories.summary: Galway native Eimear Flannery has been named at the Head of Operations for next year's Lions Women's Tour. Flannery is one of three new appointments for Lions ahead of their inaugural Tour to New Zealand in 2027. Charlie Hayter joins from the RFU and has been appointed general manager of high performance while Scotland's Josie Symonds named head of athletic performance. Flannery has already started in her role as as head of operations with the Lions, having previously served as Ireland's Women's team manager and 7s programme manager as well as rugby operations programme manager with Edinburgh Rugby. She will lead the operational and logistical delivery of the Lions Women’s Tour to ensure the touring party is fully supported throughout. "It is an honour to be joining The British & Irish Lions, and particularly to be part of the first Lions Women's Tour," Flannery said. "It is a special moment that I feel very proud to be involved in.

stories.title: This Modern Love: Emma Gilleece's ode to Irish architecture
stories.summary: 'First of all we must cleanse our minds of imitation, and, in disengaging ourselves of antique manners, bring our work to simplicity and truth shaping each building to necessity, and look for beauty in chastity and proportions. That is the task before all Irish art, and it is especially the task before Irish architecture'. This was the clarion call Darrell Figgis (1882-1925), the co-drafter of the Irish Free State’s constitution, made on 22 March 1922 in his address to the Architectural Association of Ireland. As a member of the Gaelic League, he understood cultural self-expression to extend beyond language and into the built environment. In his view, the continued reliance on the historicist architectural traditions of Britain, Ireland’s former coloniser, risked constraining the development of a distinct national identity and inhibiting the evolution of an indigenous architectural language. This presented an opportunity to project the nation’s forward-looking ambitions through a contemporary architectural language, free from the ornamentation and stylistic conventions associated with imperial rule, from early Georgian to Edwardian. Modernism was particularly well suited to a nation seeking to define itself as an independent republic, reflecting aspirations towards greater social equality, civic progress and economic self-sufficiency and even lent itself to the conservatism of the Catholic Church. This book celebrates the architects, craftspeople, artists, clients, and policymakers who embraced this vision, as well as the subsequent generations who carried forward the principles of modernism through the Free State and into the Republic. The first milestone in Irish modernity was the construction of the hydroelectric power station at Ardnacrusha, overseen by the Cumann na nGaedheal administration of the 1920s. Political and cultural transformations followed with the arrival of a Fianna Fáil government in 1932, which advanced protectionism and began an economic war (1933-7) with Britain. Among other things, this hugely affected the availability of building materials. Nevertheless, in that same year, the Housing (Financial and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act came into force to provide local authorities with state funding for the provision of houses for working class families who had been cleared from the slums of Dublin, Cork, Limerick, and Waterford. Between 1932 and 1942, despite Ireland’s economic vulnerability, 12,000 houses per year were built. Our modern hospitals also evolved at this time with the establishment of the Hospitals Trust Board to administer the funds raised by the Hospital Sweepstakes Fund. The modernist principles of hygiene, free circulation, light, and lack of ornament were perfectly suited to such buildings and the resulting hospitals came to embody the spirit of medical and architectural progress. During the ‘Emergency’, despite our neutral status, hundreds of defensive structures were rapidly built around our coast and were modernist in material and form. After the War, it was, strangely enough, the Catholic Church, the stewards of conservatism, oppression, and censorship, who would be the country’s greatest patron of modernist architecture and art in the churches built after the Second Vatican Council of 1962 to 1965. Modernist architecture seemed to symbolise a Church that was more liberal and open, more orientated to the future, and more in keeping with the outward-looking economics and ‘invitation to industrialisation’ pursued by Lemass’ government, leading to the membership of the EEC in January 1973. The scope of this research runs from 1927 to the late 1970s. This survey of fifty structures is certainly not an exhaustive list. Instead, its ambition is to draw attention to structures that are often unloved or just overlooked and to show that these can be found across the country, contradicting the common belief that architectural innovation and novelty can only be found in our capital or at least only in our major cities. Every county in the Republic of Ireland is covered by at least one structure, ranging from government buildings, schools, post offices to a handball alley, garda station, and a water tower. Some buildings are iconic (and therefore already familiar to the reader), others are little-known gems, but what they all have in common is that they are irreplaceable. Conscious that architecture is, of course, something that is best experienced in person, this book is designed to fit into your bag or the glove compartment of your car to bring on trips around the country. Such an introduction is a springboard to entice the reader to seek out these structures and, perhaps, take a deeper-dive into the history of this quite everyday built heritage. The lamentable near absence of women architects in this volume - represented by only one building out of fifty - mirrors the broader scarcity of women in Irish architecture and engineering throughout the early to mid-twentieth century. Societal expectations, restrictive marriage bars, and exclusionary professional cultures made it exceptionally difficult for women to enter, remain in, or advance within these fields. Against this backdrop, the achievement of Angela Jupe, the architect of the Braun factory in Co. Carlow stands out: leading a design team at the Industrial Development Agency (IDA) in the early 1970s was a rare and significant accomplishment for a woman in the profession. Nevertheless, the book highlights instances in which women artists made significant contributions to the overall conception and experience of architectural projects, including the façade of the Department of Trade and Enterprise and the interior artistic programme of St Aengus Church. In addition, anecdotal accounts indicate that the wives of a number of male architects, who had professions for their creativity pre-marriage, were involved in advising on interior design and landscaping schemes. Such contributions, however, were seldom recorded in official project documentation and therefore remain largely absent from the historical record. May this book be the starting point for oral histories on these undocumented contributions.

stories.title: JK Rowling 'will keep speaking out despite death threats'
stories.summary: JK Rowling has vowed to keep speaking out and financially supporting women with legal cases in the face of "trans activism", as she told how she has faced "an avalanche of death, rape and torture threats" in recent years. The Harry Potter author said she felt "shocked and disgusted" at what she described as "large numbers of women" who had "spent the last few years vilifying members of their own sex for fighting to retain their hard-won rights and single-sex spaces". Publishing an essay on the topic on Wednesday, she argued that current "trans activism" is "elitist to its core" and affects mainly women who are not in positions of privilege. She hit out at "wealthy women who repost the vogueish mantras while sitting in dressing rooms guarded by private security guards" as well as "headline-hungry female politicians". Harry Potter stars Emma Watson, Daniel Radcliffe and Rupert Grint have previously distanced themselves from Rowling's views. Last year, Rowling suggested Watson, who played Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter eight-part film series, had "so little experience of real life she’s ignorant of how ignorant she is".

stories.title: Seasoned marathon runners give their best race day tips
stories.summary: The carbs are being eaten; the hard work has been done. But what should you keep in mind on the day itself? However prepared you may feel for your first marathon, it is still a huge, amazing challenge to take on, and nerves will be inevitable. There is a reason people go on to run countless marathons, though, and there is plenty to be learned from them. So, what can we learn from seasoned long-distance runners who take on 26.2 miles time and time again? "Give yourself plenty of time to get to the start," says experienced London Marathon runner Alice Ball, "that includes enough time for one final trip to the portaloo before you have to be in your pen. Queues for portaloos for the world majors, in particular, can be long, but that final wee or more is a necessity, believe me." However many times you have run marathons, changing anything at the last minute could be a race-ruiner.

stories.title: Significant increase in young people dying on Irish roads
stories.summary: There has been a significant increase in the number of young people being killed on the country's road this year, according to new figures released by An Garda Síochána today. According to the provisional figures for 2026, 45 people aged under the age of 25 have died in road collisions so far this year; almost a third of all road traffic fatalities. This compares to 32 people aged under 25 in the same period last year. Over 65s accounted for a fifth of all road deaths (30), but made up over a third of all pedestrians who were killed (10 out of 28). A total of 149 people have been killed on the country's roads so far this year.** The number of deaths was greater than the number of actual collisions (138), with gardaí reporting that collisions resulting in multiple fatalities had significant impact on figures.

stories.title: Behind The Story: Sorry saga of signal failure
stories.summary: Even after writing off €50m, Iarnród Éireann still finds itself embroiled in a battle over a failed signalling project that could end up costing even more, despite never having been operational. Today senior management from the company were before the Oireachtas Transport Committee answering questions on how the contract for a new rail traffic management system went so badly wrong. On this episode of Behind The Story, Irish Times Public Policy Correspondent Martin Wall takes us back to the beginning of this story, which saw Spanish company Indra awarded a contract in 2020. In July this year, Iarnród Éireann terminated its contract with Indra because it had "not delivered" what was contracted for. However, that is not the end of the story. Both sides now are embroiled in a dispute over a further €30m in costs associated with the project. And on top of this, the much-needed new signalling project still needs to get done. "Irish Rail wants to bring in a new contractor, Siemens," Martin explains. "It needs to get approval from the National Transport Authority before it can actually start that process."

stories.title: Dáil hears call for 'crackdown' on drug debt intimidation
stories.summary: Sinn Féin has tabled a motion in the Dáil calling for an "immediate and determined crackdown" on drug debt intimidation. Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan thanked Sinn Féin for tabling the motion which he said the Government is supporting. The party's spokesperson on justice, Matt Carthy, introduced the motion during Private Members' Business, urging action to support communities affected by drug-related intimidation. He said that families facing threats and coercion from criminal gangs must receive the protection and support they need - along with "high-visibility policing on their streets". The deputy told the Dáil that families people are living in fear, in despair and "too often feel abandoned". "The horrific murders in Waterford ... shocked us all," he said, adding that TDs must work to ensure such a tragedy never happens again.

stories.title: Kerry Group keeps full year earnings per share guidance
stories.summary: Food technology and ingredients company Kerry Group has reported third quarter volume growth of 3.6% and said it was maintaining its constant currency adjusted earnings per share guidance of 6% to 10% growth for 2026. In an interim management statement, Kerry said volume growth in the first nine months of the year reflected continued strong end market outperformance and further progression across each of the three regions - Europe, the Americas and APMEA. Breaking down its regions, Kerry Group said that "strong" volume growth of 4% was reported in the Americas business, on the back of very good performances in both North America and LATAM. Kerry said that within North America, strong growth was achieved in snacks through innovations and renovations using its range of savoury taste profiles and Tastesense salt reduction technologies, as well as new innovations with emerging and retail brands. Within LATAM, strong growth was achieved in Mexico across Snacks and Beverage end use markets, it noted. Strategic investments in the region included beverage taste capacity and capability enhancements in North America and progression of footprint expansion for savoury taste capabilities in Mexico, it added.

stories.title: World can no longer avoid exceeding 1.5C threshold - UN
stories.summary: The world has lost the opportunity to prevent global warming significantly exceeding the critical threshold of 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, according to a major new UN report. Decades of inadequate action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions mean that a significant overshoot of the temperature limit is now unavoidable. The international community faces the much greater challenge of limiting the extent and duration of further warming and eventually bringing global temperatures back down. The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) has said global emissions would now need to fall by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, compared with 2025 levels, to keep warming to the lowest achievable overshoot of 1.5C. However, even if governments fully implement their existing national climate commitments, emissions are expected to decline by just 11% to 15% by 2035. The findings are contained in UNEP's annual Emissions Gap Report 2026, entitled The Point of Return, published ahead of next month's COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.

stories.title: Emery confident his Villa side are improving fast
stories.summary: Aston Villa boss Unai Emery believes the confidence of his players is improving after they continued their impressive start to the Champions League campaign with a 3-1 victory over Viking. Villa Park is becoming a fortress in Europe and they have now won their last 12 major European home games and made it three from three in this year's Champions League. They picked up their latest win thanks to Ross Barkley’s opener and Emi Buendia’s penalty, as well as an own goal from Henrik Heggheim. Villa would have finished the night top of the Champions League table but for Viking’s Peter Christiansen replying late which also denied them a third straight clean sheet. Emery admits there is still work to do but his side took another step forward. He said: "We are delighted how we are responding to our demands. Respecting the competition, respecting the opponents and how we are improving things.
